title: Rising Subsurface Phosphorus and Spatially  Divergent Chlorophyll Responses to Coastal Upwelling in the Bothnian Sea
content: Coastal upwelling can intermittently displace subsurface water toward productive surface layers, but irregular monitoring makes its ecological consequences difficult to distinguish from short-term cooling, mixing, and biomass displacement. This study integrates vertical hydrography, hourly ERA5 winds and sea-surface temperature (SST), satellite SST, and water-quality observations from ten stations along the eastern coast of the Bothnian Sea, a northern Baltic Sea sub-basin. Temperature, salinity, stratification, station-specific wind forcing, and SST cooling were evaluated jointly to identify physically supported upwelling events. At four coastal stations, chlorophyll-a observations were paired with total phosphorus (TP) at 10–15 m and continuous 3-, 7-, 14-, and 30-day cold-exposure indices. May–September SST increased by 0.263 °C decade⁻¹ during 1940–2026, whereas summer wind speed and the frequency of July 2026-like 72 h wind episodes showed no significant trends. Subsurface TP increased at all four coastal stations, most rapidly at Kylmäpihlaja and Vav-15, where chlorophyll-a also shifted to higher post-2010 levels. Sample-level models did not support a uniform positive chlorophyll response. Kylmäpihlaja showed a negative short-lag TP × cold-exposure interaction consistent with immediate displacement or dilution, whereas POME276 showed a positive 14-day interaction consistent with a delayed biological response, although model-selection support was limited. A July 2026 satellite case documented spatially coherent wind forcing followed by a coastal cold-water band. Rising subsurface phosphorus, rather than increasingly frequent strong regional wind forcing, therefore provides a more plausible basis for increasing ecological potential, while local hydrography and response lag condition its expression in coastal chlorophyll dynamics.
